paper.title: Virtual Node Graph Neural Network for Full Phonon Prediction
paper.research_summary: The paper introduces the Virtual Node Graph Neural Network (VGNN) to predict phonon spectra and bandstructures directly from atomic coordinates, addressing challenges of variable-length output and complex unit cells. It presents three VGNN variants—vector (VVN), matrix (MVN), and momentum-dependent matrix (k-MVN) virtual nodes—to predict Γ-point phonons and full phonon dispersion. The method is validated on alloy systems and used to build a Γ-phonon database of over 146,000 materials from the Materials Project.

tasks.objective: Direct prediction of Γ-phonon spectra and full phonon bandstructures from atomic coordinates
constraints: input limited to atomic coordinates without prior knowledge of interatomic forces
must scale to complex materials with large unit cells (up to 400+ atoms)
output_goal: 3m Γ-phonon energies for m-atom unit cell
full phonon band structure at arbitrary k points in Brillouin zone

evidence.text: By developing three types of virtual node approaches - the vector, matrix, and momentum-dependent matrix virtual nodes, we achieve direct prediction of Γ-phonon spectra and full dispersion only using atomic coordinates as input.

stages.stage_name_raw: acquisition of ab initio phonon data
stages.stage_goal: Obtain high-quality phonon dispersion data from first-principles calculations for training and validation

evidence.text: We trained all of our models against an ab initio DFPT computational database for phonon dispersion in harmonic model25.

The data set contains material structures (the same as the primitive structure obtained from the Material Project12), second-order derivatives of energies with respect to atomic perturbations for regular points inside the irreducible zone, and phonon dispersion along highly symmetric paths of 1,521 crystalline inorganic materials.

stages.stage_goal: Prepare and quality-control phonon datasets for training and testing, including complex materials with large unit cells
stage_output: complex-material test set (156 materials with >40 atoms/unit cell)

evidence.text: The data set contains material structures [...] and phonon dispersion along highly symmetric paths of 1,521 crystalline inorganic materials. These materials have 2 to 40 atoms per unit cell, with an average of 7.38. For this work, we only used the highly symmetric path phonon dispersion as our training data. All models randomly split the data into 90% training (1,365 materials), and 10% testing (156 materials) sets.

We also got phonon dispersion of complex (more number of atoms per unit cell) materials from Atsushi Togo’s phonon database31. [...] Finally, we randomly selected 156 (the same as the number of data in the testing set for ease of comparison) out of 505 ﬁltered materials. We used them as our complex material data set.

stages.stage_name_raw: training of VGNN models (VVN, MVN, k-MVN)
stages.stage_goal: Optimize neural network parameters to minimize prediction error on phonon spectra

evidence.text: The model is optimized by minimizing the mean squared error (MSE) loss function between the phonon of the training data set and the one predicted by the model after normalizing them by the maximum phonon frequency of each material.
We optimize the values of the training parameters. The set of parameters that gives the best results for VVN, MVN, k-MVN are shown in Table S1.
evidence.section: III NEURAL NETWORK TRAINING AND OPTIMIZATION

stages.stage_goal: Assess model performance on test sets using loss distribution, correlation plots, and spectral comparisons
stage_output: correlation plots (predicted vs ground-truth phonon frequencies)

evidence.text: The main results using the VVN for Γ-phonon prediction are shown in Figure 2b. The three-row spectral comparison plots are randomly selected samples from the test set within each error tertile [...] c-d. Evaluation of the test accuracy through the distribution of loss function and correlation plot between ground-truth and predicted average phonon frequencies, respectively.

The predicted phonons using MVN are summarized in Figure 3b, which shares the same structure with Figure 2b as error tertile plots [...] MVN shows comparable performance with VVN for simple materials [...] but shows signiﬁcant performance improvement for complex materials.

evidence.text: We trained all of our models against an ab initio DFPT computational database for phonon dispersion in harmonic model25.

The data set contains material structures (the same as the primitive structure obtained from the Material Project12), second-order derivatives of energies with respect to atomic perturbations for regular points inside the irreducible zone, and phonon dispersion along highly symmetric paths of 1,521 crystalline inorganic materials.

The data set containing full phonon bands of 1521 semiconducting inorganic materials are calculated from density functional perturbation theory (DFPT)?, which is the main dataset for training (“Main Database” for short).
We also got phonon dispersion of complex (more number of atoms per unit cell) materials from Atsushi Togo’s phonon database31.

Another set of data for testing the model was taken from the Phonon database by Dr. Atsuhi Togo at Kyoto University (“Togo Database” for short)?, which contains the phonons of more complex materials, but meanwhile contain more phonons with imaginary phonon energies.
Phonon database at kyoto university. http://phonondb.mtl.kyoto-u.ac.jp/, 2015.
